items.prompt: Why does the soil an earthworm has fed through often end up richer than it started?

options.label: The worm adds minerals it absorbs from its own body
options.feedback: A worm is not depositing minerals from its own tissue; whatever comes out has passed through it, not been drawn from it.

options.label: Worms attract other animals whose waste enriches the soil
options.feedback: The enrichment comes directly from the worm's own digestion, not from other animals gathering nearby.

options.label: Digestion breaks down organic matter into a more nutrient-available form
options.feedback: The worm's gut breaks apart tough organic matter and releases nutrients that were previously locked in a form roots could not use.

options.label: Tunneling exposes deeper soil that was already nutrient-rich
options.feedback: Exposing lower soil layers is not what changes the nutrient content; the worm's own digestive process is what does that.

items.ok_line: What comes out is more usable than what went in.
items.ko_title: It's the digestion, not the tunneling
items.ko_line: The enrichment happens inside the worm, before anything is left behind.
items.exp_title: Richer coming out than going in
items.exp_text: As an earthworm swallows soil and decaying leaves, its gut breaks apart tough organic matter and mixes it with its own digestive fluids, releasing nutrients that were previously locked up in a form plant roots could not use. What passes out the other end, its casting, is left far more available to plants than the material the worm originally ate.

items.prompt: How does an earthworm get the oxygen it needs, since it has no lungs at all?

options.label: Oxygen diffuses in through its moist skin
options.feedback: Oxygen dissolves into the mucus coating the worm's skin and passes directly through into the blood vessels just beneath it.

options.label: It gulps air through its mouth like a fish gulps water
options.feedback: A worm's mouth is used for feeding, not for taking in air; nothing about its digestive opening handles gas exchange.

options.label: It stores oxygen in an internal air sac
options.feedback: A worm has no internal reservoir of air; whatever oxygen it uses has to be taken in continuously, not stored ahead of time.

options.label: It surfaces at night to breathe directly
options.feedback: Coming to the surface at night is mostly about moisture and movement, not about needing open air to breathe — the skin can take in oxygen underground just as well.

items.ok_line: Every bit of its surface is doing the breathing.
items.ko_title: No mouth, no sac, no surfacing needed
items.ko_line: The gas exchange happens continuously, across the whole moist surface of its body.
items.exp_text: An earthworm's thin skin is kept constantly damp by mucus, and oxygen from the air trapped in the soil dissolves into that moisture and then passes directly through the skin into the worm's blood vessels just beneath it. Because this exchange only works while the skin stays wet, a worm stranded on dry pavement suffocates even surrounded by air that is otherwise full of oxygen.

items.prompt: How does an earthworm push its way forward through solid soil?

options.label: It dissolves the soil in front of it with saliva
options.feedback: A worm does not dissolve soil chemically to move through it; its progress comes from a physical, muscular action instead.

options.label: It spins its whole body like a drill
options.feedback: A worm's movement is not a rotating, drilling motion; it advances by a very different kind of muscular action.

options.label: Tiny claws on its head dig a path ahead of it
options.feedback: A worm has no claws at all; what grips the soil as it moves is a different, much simpler structure spread along its whole body.

options.label: Bristles grip the soil while waves of muscle contraction pull it forward
options.feedback: Bristles anchor part of the body while a wave of muscle contraction lengthens and pulls the rest of the worm forward to catch up.

items.ok_line: Grip, then pull — repeated down the whole body.
items.ko_title: No claws, no drilling, no dissolving
items.ko_line: The real mechanism is a simple pairing of tiny bristles and muscle contractions.
items.exp_text: Along the underside of its body an earthworm carries rows of tiny bristles called setae, and it moves by contracting circular muscles to make part of its body thin and long while anchoring itself with bristles farther back, then contracting lengthwise muscles to pull the rest of its body forward to catch up. This wave of contraction travels down the worm from one end to the other, and repeating it again and again is what drives the worm steadily through the soil.

items.prompt: What ultimately happens to a fallen leaf that lies on damp forest soil long enough?

options.label: It slowly turns to stone
options.feedback: Turning to stone takes conditions and timescales far beyond anything an ordinary forest floor provides; that is not the fate of an ordinary fallen leaf.

options.label: Decomposers break it down into the dark material called humus
options.feedback: Bacteria, fungi, and small soil animals break the leaf's tissue into smaller fragments, leaving behind the dark, nutrient-rich humus.

options.label: It is absorbed whole by nearby tree roots
options.feedback: A root cannot take in a whole leaf; it can only absorb small dissolved substances, which the leaf has to be broken down into first.

options.label: Rain washes it away before anything can happen to it
options.feedback: Some leaves are washed elsewhere, but plenty stay in place long enough to be broken down right where they fell.

items.ok_line: The leaf becomes part of the ground it fell on.
items.ko_title: Not stone, not swallowed whole, not just washed away
items.ko_line: Something is actively breaking the leaf apart, piece by piece.
items.exp_text: Bacteria, fungi, and small soil animals all feed on a fallen leaf at once, each one breaking its tough plant tissue into smaller and smaller fragments and releasing the nutrients locked inside as they do. What remains after enough of this feeding is a dark, crumbly material called humus, no longer recognizable as a leaf but rich in exactly the nutrients a growing plant needs.

items.prompt: How do certain plants get nitrogen they can use, when the nitrogen gas filling the air around them is not something a root can absorb directly?

options.label: Rain dissolves nitrogen gas directly into a form roots absorb
options.feedback: Rain does not convert nitrogen gas into a usable form; nitrogen gas is far too unreactive to be pulled into raindrops that way.

options.label: The plant filters nitrogen straight out of the air through its leaves
options.feedback: A leaf cannot pull nitrogen gas out of the air and turn it into a usable form; that conversion needs a living partner, not a leaf acting alone.

options.label: Bacteria living in nodules on its roots convert the gas into a usable form
options.feedback: Inside root nodules, bacteria break apart nitrogen gas and combine it into compounds the plant can actually absorb, in exchange for sugar.

options.label: Lightning near the plant converts nitrogen gas for it every time it strikes
options.feedback: Lightning can convert some atmospheric nitrogen generally, but it is not something that happens reliably for an individual plant whenever it needs nitrogen.

items.ok_line: Bacteria do the chemistry the plant cannot.
items.ko_title: Not rain, not leaves, not lightning
items.ko_line: The plant relies on a living partner working inside its own roots.
items.exp_title: A converter living inside the roots
items.exp_text: Certain bacteria settle inside small swellings called nodules on a plant's roots, and inside those nodules they carry out a chemical conversion no plant cell can perform on its own, breaking apart the tightly bonded nitrogen gas and combining it into compounds the plant can actually absorb. In exchange for this service the plant supplies the bacteria with sugar from its own leaves, a trade that lets both partners get something they could not obtain alone.

items.prompt: Why does topsoil usually look darker than the paler soil layers found deeper down?

options.label: It is mixed with humus, the dark remains of decomposed matter
options.feedback: Constant decomposition near the surface leaves dark, crumbly humus worked into the topsoil, which the deeper layers rarely receive.

options.label: It stays wetter than the layers below it
options.feedback: Extra dampness alone would not turn soil dark; the actual color change comes from what is mixed into it, not how wet it is.

options.label: Minerals near the surface are naturally darker in color
options.feedback: The minerals in topsoil are largely the same ones found in the paler layers beneath it; the difference in color is not coming from the minerals themselves.

options.label: Sunlight darkens the exposed top layer over time
options.feedback: Sunlight does not darken soil the way it might tan skin; the color of topsoil has nothing to do with sun exposure.

items.ok_line: The dark color is decomposed matter mixed right into the ground.
items.ko_title: It isn't water, minerals, or sunlight
items.ko_line: Look for something added into the topsoil that the deeper layers never receive.
items.exp_title: Darkened by what has decomposed into it
items.exp_text: Topsoil sits closest to the surface, where fallen leaves, dead roots, and other organic matter are constantly being broken down by decomposers and worked into the ground, leaving behind the dark, crumbly humus that colors the soil around it. Deeper layers receive almost none of this decomposed material, since it rarely gets carried or mixed that far down, which is why they stay pale by comparison.

items.prompt: Why do plant roots grow thousands of extremely fine hairs near their tips?

options.label: The hairs anchor the plant more firmly against wind
options.feedback: Firm anchoring against wind comes mainly from the thicker main roots, not from these fine, fragile hairs.

options.label: The hairs store extra sugar for the plant to use later
options.feedback: Root hairs are not a storage structure; they are too thin and short-lived to hold any meaningful reserve of sugar.

options.label: The hairs protect the growing root tip from damage
options.feedback: The delicate growing tip itself is actually shielded by a separate cap of cells, not by the root hairs, which grow farther back.

options.label: The hairs increase the surface area available for absorbing water and minerals
options.feedback: Thousands of hairs multiply the root's contact with damp soil far beyond what its own surface alone could provide.

items.ok_line: Thousands of hairs multiply how much of the soil the root can touch.
items.ko_line: The hairs exist to increase contact with the soil around them.
items.exp_title: Surface area multiplied many times over
items.exp_text: Each root hair is a single, greatly elongated cell that reaches out into the tiny gaps between soil particles, and because a root produces so many of these hairs close together near its tip, the total surface area in contact with damp soil becomes far larger than the root's own surface alone could ever provide. Water and dissolved minerals move into the plant through this vastly expanded contact area, which is why a plant can gather what it needs from soil that looks, to the eye, mostly dry.

items.prompt: How can a seed buried in the soil survive for years before finally sprouting?

options.label: It stays a living plant the entire time, just too small to see
options.feedback: A dormant seed is not a tiny, actively growing plant the whole time; its growth is essentially paused, not simply invisible.

options.label: A tough coat and a paused metabolism let it wait for the right conditions
options.feedback: With its internal processes slowed nearly to a stop and a tough coat sealing out water and oxygen, the seed barely ages until conditions finally line up.

options.label: It slowly converts into a different kind of seed while buried
options.feedback: A buried seed does not transform into a different kind of seed; it stays the same seed, simply inactive, until conditions trigger it.

options.label: Underground temperatures keep it perfectly preserved like a refrigerator
options.feedback: Underground temperature alone does not explain the seed's survival; the seed's own protective coat and paused internal processes are what do the work.

items.ok_line: A paused plant, sealed and ready.
items.ko_title: It isn't already growing, transforming, or just being chilled
items.ko_line: The seed has essentially stopped its own processes until something tells it to start.
items.exp_title: A pause built into the seed itself
items.exp_text: A dormant seed wraps its embryo in a tough outer coat that keeps out water and oxygen, and with its internal processes slowed to almost nothing, the tiny plant inside barely ages while it waits. Only when conditions finally line up — enough moisture reaching the embryo, the coat softening or cracking, the right temperature holding steady — does the seed's growth resume and a seedling finally break through the soil.

items.prompt: How does a mole manage to catch worms and insects while tunneling through complete underground darkness?

options.label: It memorizes the layout of its tunnels visually before the dark sets in
options.feedback: A mole's eyesight is extremely poor to begin with, so relying on a visual memory of the tunnel layout would not help it hunt in true darkness.

options.label: It listens for the faint sounds prey make while burrowing nearby
options.feedback: Sound plays some role for many burrowing animals, but a mole's actual hunting relies on a far more immediate sense than listening for distant noise.

options.label: It relies on an extremely touch-sensitive snout to feel out prey
options.feedback: Thousands of touch-sensitive receptors on its snout let the mole locate and seize prey the instant it brushes against one, without needing to see it.

options.label: It follows scent trails left in the air of the tunnel
options.feedback: Airborne scent spreads poorly through the tight, still air of a tunnel; a mole's hunting depends on direct contact rather than tracking a scent through the air.

items.ok_line: In the dark, touch does the job eyes cannot.
items.ko_line: The mole's real advantage is an extraordinarily sensitive sense of touch.
items.exp_title: A snout built to feel, not see
items.exp_text: A mole's snout is covered in touch-sensitive receptors that can register the faintest vibration or contact against it, far more finely than the whiskers or skin of most other animals. As the mole pushes through its tunnel, it sweeps this snout continuously ahead of itself, and the instant it brushes against a worm or grub it can locate and seize the prey without ever needing to see it at all.

items.prompt: Why do earthworm tunnels benefit more than just the worm that dug them?

options.label: They create channels that let air and water reach deep into the soil
options.feedback: The open tunnel gives air and rainwater a direct route down to depths they would otherwise reach only slowly by seeping through solid ground.

options.label: They release chemicals that fertilize the surrounding soil
options.feedback: The tunnels themselves release no chemicals; whatever fertilizing effect exists comes from the worm's castings, not from the empty tunnel walls.

options.label: They trap heat that keeps deeper soil warm in winter
options.feedback: An open tunnel does not trap heat any better than solid soil; if anything, it lets cold air move more freely, not less.

options.label: They collect rainwater in pools that other animals drink from
options.feedback: A worm tunnel drains rather than holds standing water; it is not built or shaped to collect a pool.

items.ok_line: A path the worm dug becomes a path for air, water, and roots too.
items.ko_title: Not chemicals, warmth, or standing water
items.ko_line: The real benefit is the open channel itself, running down through the soil.
items.exp_title: A channel left open for others
items.exp_text: An earthworm's tunnel remains as an open passage through the soil long after the worm has moved on, giving air and rainwater a direct route down to depths they would otherwise reach only slowly by seeping through solid ground. Plant roots often follow these same channels downward since they offer far less resistance than undisturbed soil, and other small soil creatures use them as ready-made corridors of their own.
